name: Work at the Trestle
desc:
The Artist
Ruth Abernethy is an internationally renowned Canadian artist and sculptor. Her commissioned bronze pieces include figure portraits of Sir John A. Macdonald, Queen Elizabeth II, Glenn Gould, Oscar Peterson, and Abraham Lincoln. Ruth’s sculptures are installed and have become iconic on sites municipally, regionally and nationally.

The Piece
Work at the Trestle (2013, bronze) features a figure portrait of T.T. Vernon Smith, civil engineer and builder of the Windsor and Annapolis Railway, which operated from 1869 to 1894. Ruth has imagined Smith throwing together an emergency workstation. He pores over his map, agonizing over miles of new railway lines washed out to sea by the Saxby Gale of 1869.

The Location
Waterfront Park, Wolfville, Nova Scotia

Disclaimer
teaser_description: Listen to Ruth Abernethy's invitation to visit the sculpture and learn more.

name: Dominion Atlantic Railroad
desc:
The Artist
Edwin Hollett is a long-time Kings County artist known for his seascapes and paintings of tall ships. Working mostly in watercolours and acrylics, he also paints historical scenes and buildings from vintage photographs and his own research. In 2017, Edwin completed a second mural, depicting buildings from historic Kentville, on the opposite side of the warehouse wall that displays the railway mural.

The Piece
The Dominion Atlantic Railway, Kentville (2011, exterior oil paint) is a 60 foot (18.3 metre) mural commemorating the Kentville train station. While this scene of a steam locomotive and its passenger cars pulling in to the station is from the 1930s, the DAR ran for 100 years from 1894 to 1994. Corporate headquarters were in London, UK, and then Montreal, but its operational headquarters were always in Kentville.

The Location
Station Lane, Kentville, Nova Scotia

name: Acadian Deportation Cross
desc:
The Artist
René-Arthur Fréchet (1879–1950) was a Montreal-born architect. After earning a degree in architecture from Laval University in 1898, he became involved in the Acadian community when he married Elvina Cormier in 1903. Fréchet also designed the Memorial Church at Grand Pré, which was completed in 1922 as a place of remembrance for the Acadian people.

The Piece
The Deportation Cross (1924, wrought iron) commemorates the deportation of thousands of Acadians from this spot in 1755. Forged from wrought iron in the Gothic style, the cross symbolizes the Trinity, hope, the universe, and violence. When the cross was first unveiled, it was a pilgrimage marker beside the Dominion Atlantic Railway tracks; it was moved to its present location in 2005.

The Location
Horton Landing, Hortonville, Nova Scotia

name: Disruptor
desc:
The Artist
Ruth Abernethy is an internationally renowned Canadian artist and sculptor. Her commissioned bronze pieces include figure portraits of Sir John A. Macdonald, Queen Elizabeth II, Glenn Gould, Oscar Peterson, and Abraham Lincoln. Ruth’s sculptures are installed and have become iconic on sites municipally, regionally and nationally.

The Piece
Disruptor (2019, bronze, concrete, stainless steel) shows a figure portrait of Abraham Gesner (1797–1864) within a multifaceted sculpture more than 10 metres across. Gesner was a disruptor – the inventor of kerosene and a man ahead of his time. As you walk around the design, you can read about his compelling life. And you’ll want to find out what that whale tail is doing there.

The Location
Chipman’s Corner, Middle Dyke Road, Port Williams, Nova Scotia

name: The Joy is Almost Too Much to Bear
desc:
The Artist

Nistal Prem de Boer was born in Amsterdam and immigrated to Canada after earning a degree in architecture and engineering. In 1976 he moved from Montreal to Nova Scotia where,as an independent architect, he designed solar houses.In 1988 he moved to Italy,returning to Nova Scotia in 1999. His lifelong love affair with sculpture became his professional ambition, and he now creates sculptures in bronze

The Piece

The Joy is Almost Too Much to Bear (2017, bronze) are words Mona Parsons wrote to her father following her liberation from the Nazis in 1945. A Nova Scotia war hero, Mona saved the lives of Allied airmen in Occupied Holland until she was betrayed and imprisoned in 1941.When she escaped four years later, ill and starving, she walked 200 kilometers to safety. Thesculpture captures her moment of liberation.

The Location

Post Office, Wolfville, Nova Scotia

name: Dr. Apple
desc:
The Artist
 Ruth Abernethy is an internationally renowned Canadian artist and sculptor. Her commissioned bronze pieces include figure portraits of Sir John A. Macdonald, Queen Elizabeth II, Glenn Gould, Oscar Peterson, andAbraham Lincoln. Ruth’s sculptures are installed and have become iconic on sites municipally, regionally and nationally.

The Piece
Dr. Apple (2015, bronze) features a figure portrait of fruit scientist Charles Eaves (1908–2006), who created North America's first atmospherically controlled fruit storage in 1939. Beside him are the wooden apple boxes and barrel that were part of the Valley’s apple-growing landscape. Those who knew Eaves speak of him warmly. Can you see the twinkle in his eye?

The Location
Eaves Hollow (across from the Research and Development Centre), Kentville, Nova Scotia

name: Fountain of Grand-Pré
desc:
The Artist
 Willy Dinner was born in the St. Gallen Rhine Valley region of Switzerland. He worked in the financial sector of a Swiss company for thirty-five years before leaving to focus on art. A mountaineer, filmmaker and pilot, he sees painting as an opportunity to share his experiences and portray what fascinates him. He is proud of the stone artwork he created in Nova Scotia.

The Piece
Fountain of Grand Pré (1998, basalt and stainless steel) is a trickling fountain of three rock columns linked to one another and to a central steel pole. For the artist, the basalt represents the mystery of its ancient volcanic origins, and the water represents life. But the elements of the fountain also represent the family who rebuilt and reopened the winery, and the wine that flows from there to the world. (The narrator is Cäcilia Stutz, a member of the family that owns and operates the winery.)


The Location
Domaine de Grand Pré, Grand Pré, Nova Scotia

name: Statue of Evangeline
desc:
The Artist
Louis-Philippe Hébert (1850–1917) was a respected Quebec artist of Acadian ancestry. He designed the statue of Evangeline and produced a model of it shortly before his death. In 1920, his son Henri Hébert, a renowned sculptor in his own right, was commissioned by the Dominion Atlantic Railway to produce a bronze statue from the model.

The Piece
Evangeline (1920, bronze) is the most famous statue of Evangeline in the world. It depicts the fictional Acadian heroine of Evangeline: A Tale of Acadie – an 1847 poem by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow. Longfellow based the poem on a story he had heard of young lovers who were parted by the 1755 deportation of the Acadians and reunited only at the end of their lives.

The Location
Grand-Pré National Historic Site of Canada, Grand Pré, Nova Scotia

Disclaimer

name: The Tide Flows
desc:
The Artists

Michael Burt and Daniel Burt are brothers from Halifax who create art together professionally. Michael owns and operates Trackside Studios, which employs East Coast artists. Daniel has been working with him full-time for about two years. Michael describes himself as an activist for painting legal walls – walls that artists may legally paint on to practise their skills and to learn, in constant rotation, as they add to a city’s vibrancy.

The Piece

The Wolfville 125 Mural (“The Tide Flows”) (2018, acrylic spray paint) was commissioned to mark the town of Wolfville’s 125th anniversary of incorporation. Painted on the side of the Herbin Jewellers building, the mural captures words from the poetry of John Frederic Herbin (1860–1923), who established the business in 1885. The artists paid close attention to the contours of the wall as they incorporated iconic local features–such as chimney swifts flying out of the chimney.

The Location

Wolfville, Nova Scotia

Disclaimer

name: Indeterminate Tillage
desc:
The Artist
 Ericka Walker is an Associate Professor of Fine Arts at the Nova Scotia College of Art and Design. Her work is housed in public, teaching, and private collections in Canada, the United States, Europe, and Asia. Her current work refers to early 20th century propaganda imagery as an aesthetic platform for addressing historical and contemporary attitudes toward interrelated notions of war, patriotism, colonialism, agriculture, and industry.

The Piece
Indeterminate Tillage (2016, exterior latex paint) brings to mind the colourful early 20th century murals on farm buildings throughout North America.The words on the mural – “gradual tones of labour cease” – are taken from a 1921 poem by Amelia Johnston Weatherbe, a local writer. Although the poem evokes an idealized pastoral scene, the work points to the difficulties of honouring our multi-faceted heritage.

This piece was installed as part of Uncommon Common Art. Included here with permission.


The Location
Tap Root Farms, Port Williams, Nova Scotia

Disclaimer

name: That You May Live
desc:
The Artist
 Ericka Walker is an Associate Professor of Fine Arts at the Nova Scotia College of Art and Design. Her work is housed in public, teaching, and private collections in Canada, the United States, Europe, and Asia. Her current work refers to early 20th century propaganda imagery as an aesthetic platform for addressing historical and contemporary attitudes toward interrelated notions of war, patriotism, colonialism, agriculture, and industry.

The Piece
That You May Live (2018, exterior latex paint) hearkens back to the early 20th century, when colourful murals on farm buildings dotted the North American landscape. The text on the two panels, “Be Industrious That You May Live,” is the 1806 motto of the Kings County Agricultural Society. The work hints at threads between our past, our present, and our future.

This piece was installed as part of Uncommon Common Art. Included here with permission.

The Location
Longspell Point Farm, Kingsport, Nova Scotia.

name: Pasture Gate
desc:
The Artist
 Brad Hall is a sculptor and a blacksmith. He works in metal, stone and wood to create designs that combine art and function – to be enduring while rooted in the past. He has also worked in photography, pottery, weaving and the restoration of heritage buildings. Brad is a graduate of Ontario’s Sheridan School of Art.

The Piece
Pasture Gate (2015, forged steel) is placed in a wetland that used to be farm pasture. Where there are pastures, there are gates. This non-confining gate brings to mind the ways that we as humans gate our thoughts and our understanding. Its moving pieces remind us that our lives are changing all the time.

This piece was installed as part of Uncommon Common Art. Included here with permission.

The Location
Miner’s Marsh, Kentville, Nova Scotia

name: Harold Lothrop Borden Monument
desc:
The Artist

Hamilton MacCarthy (1846–1939) was an early master of monumental bronze sculpture in Canada. Born in London, England, he moved to Toronto in 1885. Thirteen years later, he moved to Ottawa, where he studied at the Royal Canadian Academy of Arts and was made a member of Council. His work appears in galleries and public spaces throughout Canada, including on Parliament Hill and at Nova Scotia’s Province House.

The Piece

The Harold Lothrop Borden Monument (1903, bronze) honours Harold Lothrop Borden, “a splendid young man of great promise” who is described as the most famous Canadian casualty of the Second Boer War. Harold was the son of Canada’s then Minister of Defence and Militia and was related to future prime minister Robert Laird Borden. He died in South Africa in 1900, age 24. (The narrator is Dr. Gordon Callon, Professor Emeritus of History, Theory, and Musicology, Acadia University).

The Location

Canning, Nova Scotia

Disclaimer

name: Emergency Exit
desc:
The Artists
 Nicole Evans first expressed herself in visual arts when she, Patrick Farrell, and Terry Drahos created the mysterious Twig People of Wolfville in 2005. The year-long adventure was so creatively fulfilling and so much fun that when she was approached to contribute to Uncommon Common Art she leapt at it. Patrick Farrell studied at the Vancouver School of Art and the Kootenay School of Art. After graduating he opened a graphic art studio and designed and built houses. Upon moving east, he returned to drawing and sculpting. He also restores historic buildings.

The Piece
Emergency Exit (2018, found door, wood, and welded steel) creates the illusion of a flying door, with the sky as its backdrop. Like so much of Nicole and Patrick’s art, it starts with a found object and a germ of an idea. Whether they’re working with a door, a piano or a car, their artwork is the culmination of intense planning and precise engineering.

This piece was installed as part of Uncommon Common Art. Included here with permission.


The Location
Grand Pré, Nova Scotia

Disclaimer

name: Charles Macdonald Concrete House Museum
desc:
The Artist
Charles Macdonald (1874–1967) was known as Nova Scotia’s Uncommon Common Man. Born in Steam Mill, Nova Scotia, he pursued artistic endeavours all his life. Charles was a sailor, a sculptor, a painter, a builder, a manufacturer, and a socialist. He also devoted much of his life to manufacturing, using, and promoting concrete. The Charles Macdonald House of Centreville Society celebrates the life and work of this exceptional Nova Scotian.


The Piece
Charles Macdonald Concrete House Museum (1916, reinforced concrete) was the home of Charles Macdonald and his wife, Mabel Misnor. Charles built the house entirely of concrete, in his own unique style, with decorative features and whimsical touches influenced by his travels in South America and the Mediterranean. While you’re here, wander among his sculpted animals on the lawn. (The narrator is Fred Macdonald, Charles’s great-nephew.)

The Location
Centreville, Nova Scotia

Disclaimer
teaser_description: Listen to Fred Macdonald’s invitation to visit the museum and learn more.

name: Aylesford in Times Gone By
desc:
The Artist
 Larry Lee has been painting murals for more than 35 years. A self-taught artist, he was one of the first to paint murals on windows in Halifax, and he still creates window paintings for businesses in the Annapolis Valley. Larry’s murals can be found in many parts of Nova Scotia and as far away as Saint Pierre and Miquelon.

The Piece
Aylesford in Times Gone By (2013, acrylic paint) is a mural that depicts historical buildings, places, and people from the town of Aylesford in the mid-20th century. Painted on a retaining wall that’s 200 feet (60 metres) long, this finely detailed mural took the artist two years to complete and was painted freehand without preliminary sketches.

The Location
Aylesford, Nova Scotia

Disclaimer

name: Untitled Stone Head
desc:
Stone head


The Artist

Brent Reeve has been creating stone art in Nova Scotia for the past eight years. Based near Berwick, he has created upwards of 100 pieces on wooded trails and within the town. He likes natural granite for its durability and timelessness.


The Piece

This untitled stone carving is one of many that Brent Reeve has created in and around Berwick. Some are hidden deep in the woods, but others, like this one, are within the town. He plays with the light. This carved head is lit by the sun in the morning but is in shadow at dusk. And the season and weather – even clouds moving across the sun – can change our perception.


The Location
Berwick, Nova Scotia
